newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Subversion law passes first hurdle in HK legislature.
newsitem.headline: Subversion law passes first hurdle in HK legislature.

text.p: Hong Kong's anti-subversion bill, which has infuriated the British colony's future sovereign power, China, passed its first hurdle in the Legislative Council on Wednesday.

The draft bill amending Hong Kong's crimes ordinance covers subversion, secession, sedition and treason. By making clear the offences entail violence and not mere oral dissent, the bill sets legal markers against China-style jailings of dissidents.
China, which takes over the territory at midnight next June 30 and plans to dissolve the elected Legislative Council, has condemned the bill.
The council decided on Wednesday to send the bill to committee debate, a procedural move that now puts it in the queue of pending legislation to be tackled in the weeks ahead.
The council's house committee will decide the next step on Friday.
British officials said they believed the bill had a good chance of passing, pro-China lawmakers vowed to vote against it and some pro-democracy independents had mixed feelings.
The colonial government argues it has the Hong Kong people's backing for the law and that it does not breach a post-1997 Hong Kong constitution promulgated by China known as the Basic Law.

"It is quite clear it is in the view of the community, as reflected by this council, that we should seek to have legislation on these concepts covering article 23 in the Basic Law before July 1, 1997," Security Secretary Peter Lai told the legislature as he presented the bill on Wednesday.
He warned legislators would have a lot of explaining to do if they vetoed the bill.
"If (the council) chooses the latter course, it would, of course, have to explain to the people of Hong Kong why it chooses that course," Lai said.
Liberal Party legislator Allen Lee attacked colonial Governor Chris Patten for introducing the bill.
"I think this is totally irresponsible," Lee told Hong Kong government radio. "He is playing politics, and he doesn't deserve to be the governor of Hong Kong."
Independent pro-democracy legislator Christine Loh said she welcomed debate on the bill but said it was too early to say whether the bill ought to become law.

"It's a good thing," Loh told Reuters during the legislative session. "It's about time we started talking in real concrete terms about ideas like subversion, which Hong Kong people are extremely unfamiliar with and which they are very fearful of."
Asked if she would like the bill to become law, she said: "I can't say. I'm glad we have a chance to discuss it, but I have not considered the merits of what is actually proposed."
